citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

These are conventions for constructed and formal calculations in this page pair. They are not empirical claims, physical postulates, or existence claims about an interacting continuum theory.

Use the geometric spacetime metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and the time coordinate $x^0=ct$ in metres. For Clifford algebra and momentum contraction use the separate algebraic metric $h=-\eta=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$; a slash or a square of an energy four-vector uses $h$, never $\eta$.

A physical energy four-vector is $p=(E,c\mathbf p_{\rm phys})$, with each component in joules. Write $M=mc^2$ for rest energy in joules and $p^2=h(p,p)=E^2-c^2|\mathbf p_{\rm phys}|^2$. For two such vectors, $s=(p_1+p_2)^2$ is in $\mathrm J^2$. Natural momentum coordinates are the energy-vector components divided by $\hbar c$, in $\mathrm m^{-1}$; they are not substituted into SI formulas without restoring this factor. In the common natural-unit field convention, $\mu=mc/\hbar$ is in $\mathrm m^{-1}$, a scalar field has dimension $\mathrm m^{-1}$, and a Dirac field has dimension $\mathrm m^{-3/2}$.

Take SI $e>0$ in coulombs, $\hbar>0$ in joule-seconds, $c>0$ in metres per second, and $\epsilon_0=(\mu_0c^2)^{-1}$. Define
$$\alpha=\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0\hbar c},\qquad g=e\sqrt{\frac{\mu_0c}{\hbar}}=\sqrt{4\pi\alpha}>0.$$
Here $g$ is a dimensionless coupling. It is not the metric and not a gyromagnetic factor.

For gauge notation set $A_{\rm lower}=(-\phi/c,\mathbf A)$, with $A_a$ in tesla-metres and gauge function $\chi$ in webers. With charge $q$ in coulombs define
$$D_a=\partial_a-\frac{iqA_a}{\hbar},\qquad \psi\mapsto e^{iq\chi/\hbar}\psi,\qquad A\mapsto A+d\chi.$$
For the electron parameter use $q=-e$. The equivalent natural-unit coordinates are $A_{\rm nat}=A_{\rm SI}/\sqrt{\mu_0\hbar c}$ and $q_{\rm nat}=q_{\rm SI}\sqrt{\mu_0c/\hbar}$.

Finite-matrix examples act on $\mathbb C^d$ with the operator norm. For Hilbert spaces, use the first-variable-linear pairing $(u,v)_1=v^\dagger u$; a displayed coordinate contraction $u^\dagger v$ is second-variable-linear and equals $\overline{(u,v)_1}$. Thus norms, traces, and modulus-squared amplitudes agree under conversion, although the unsquared pairing is conjugated. No amplitude is assigned a probability by these conventions.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every radius $R>0$ and every
nonnegative Borel function $\varphi:[0,R]\to[0,\infty]$, with extended
Lebesgue integrals and the convention $0\cdot\infty=0$,
$$ \int_{\{x\in\mathbb R^4:\ |x|\le R\}}\varphi(|x|)\,d\lambda_4(x) =2\pi^2\int_0^R\varphi(r)r^3\,dr. $$
In particular, the radial Jacobian and angular factor on a four-dimensional
ball are $r^3$ and $2\pi^2$, respectively.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every
point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$
this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable
on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then

$$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

**Both hypotheses are needed and neither is removable.** A function may be
differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does
not exist (an everywhere differentiable function with unbounded derivative) — and an
integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything
(the sign function); both witnesses are on the
companion page.

**No continuity of $f$ is assumed**, which is what makes this the working form:
the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.
For every $z\in\mathbb C$, the series $\sum z^n/n!$ converges absolutely.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

For all $z,w\in\mathbb C$, $\exp(z+w)=\exp z\exp w$. For real $x$, the complex value $\exp(x+0i)$ equals the published real exponential $e^x$. The conventions and prerequisite facts used below are recorded in [[def-complex-exponential]], [[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]], [[lem-cauchy-product-of-absolutely-convergent-complex-series]], [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]], [[lem-binomial-theorem-over-complex-numbers]], [[thm-binomial-closed-formula]].

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $u, v : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at
every point of $[a,b]$ as functions on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Suppose
$u'$ and $v'$ are integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $uv'$
and $u'v$ are integrable and

$$\int_a^b u\,v' \;=\; u(b)v(b) - u(a)v(a) \;-\; \int_a^b u'\,v .$$

**The integrability of $u'$ and $v'$ is a hypothesis, not a formality.** Without
it the two integrals in the display need not exist at all, and the identity is
then not false but ill-formed; that is
the false statement that deletes it on the companion
page. The hypothesis is automatic when $u$ and $v$ are continuously
differentiable, since a continuous function on $[a,b]$ is integrable
([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]]).

Powers are those of [[def-integer-power]], and $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to
\mathbb{R}$ is the canonical natural of [[def-canonical-natural]], so that
$\iota(0) = 0$ and $\iota(m+1) = \iota(m) + 1$. Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

1. The function $p_0 : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $p_0(x) = x^{0}$, is the
   constant function $1$, and it is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$
   with $p_0'(c) = 0$ ([[def-derivative]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$ the function $p_n : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$,
   $p_n(x) = x^{n}$, is differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and
   $$p_n'(c) \;=\; \iota(n)\,c^{\,n-1} .$$
3. For $n \ge 1$ put $A_0 := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ne 0 \,\}$. The function
   $m_n : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $m_n(x) = x^{-n}$, is differentiable at every
   $c \in A_0$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$m_n'(c) \;=\; -\,\iota(n)\,c^{\,-n-1} .$$
4. Let $a : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$ with $a_j = 0$ for $j \ge n$, and let
   $P : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be the polynomial function
   $P(x) = \sum_{j<n} a_j x^{j}$ ([[def-finite-sum]]). Then $P$ is
   differentiable at every $c \in \mathbb{R}$, and, defining $e : \mathbb{N}
   \to \mathbb{R}$ by $e_0 := 0$ and $e_j := \iota(j)\,a_j\,c^{\,j-1}$ for
   $j \ge 1$,
   $$P'(c) \;=\; \sum_{j<n} e_j .$$

**Claim 2 is stated for $n \ge 1$ and not for $n \ge 0$, and that is not
timidity.** At $n = 0$ its right-hand side reads $\iota(0)\,c^{-1}$, and
$c^{-1}$ is not defined at $c = 0$ ([[def-integer-power]]), so the formula is
not a statement about the whole line. Claim 1 is what covers $n = 0$, and it
says the derivative is $0$ there, which is what the informal reading
"$0 \cdot c^{-1}$" is reaching for. The same shift is why the term $e_0$ of
claim 4 is defined to be $0$ outright rather than by the formula.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a\in\mathbb R$ and let
$f:[a,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ be Riemann integrable on every compact interval
$[a,R]$ with $R>a$. If the improper Riemann integral
$$\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx$$
converges in the sense of [[def-improper-integral-at-infinity]], then $f$ is
Lebesgue integrable on $[a,\infty)$ and
$$\int_{[a,\infty)} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^\infty f(x)\,dx.$$

derivations.claim:
The integrand $r\mapsto r^3/(r^2+\mu^2)$ is nonnegative and continuous on
$[0,\Lambda]$. Apply [F2], then divide by $(2\pi)^4$, to obtain
$$ I_\Lambda=\frac{1}{8\pi^2}\int_0^\Lambda \frac{r^3}{r^2+\mu^2}\,dr. $$
Polynomial division gives
$r^3/(r^2+\mu^2)=r-\mu^2r/(r^2+\mu^2)$. By [F4], an antiderivative is
$G(r)=r^2/2-(\mu^2/2)\log(r^2+\mu^2)$ on this interval. Its derivative is
continuous; its compact-interval integrands are bounded and Riemann integrable, so [F9] identifies their Lebesgue integrals with the calculus integrals. Thus [F3] evaluates the integral as
$$ G(\Lambda)-G(0) =\frac12\left(\Lambda^2-\mu^2\log(1+\Lambda^2/\mu^2)\right). $$
Multiplying by $1/(8\pi^2)$ gives the claimed expression.

By [F6], $-e^{-x}$ has derivative $e^{-x}$; [F3] on $[0,R]$
gives $\int_0^R e^{-x}dx=1-e^{-R}$. The positive series [F5] gives
$e^R\ge1+R$, so $e^{-R}\to0$ and $M_0=1$.
For each integer $n\ge0$, [F5] with $y=x/2$ gives
$x^ne^{-x}\le2^n n!e^{-x/2}$. The majorant has finite integral $2^{n+1}n!$
by [F3] and [F6]; the positive truncated integrals are increasing and bounded by this finite integral, hence have a finite improper limit. All the integrands are continuous on every compact interval; [F9] identifies these convergent nonnegative improper integrals with their half-line Lebesgue integrals. Thus $M_n=\int_0^\infty x^ne^{-x}dx$ is finite.
The same bound and $e^{x/2}\ge1+x/2$ show $x^ne^{-x}\to0$.
For $n\ge1$ and $R>0$, take $u(x)=x^n$, $v(x)=-e^{-x}$ on $[0,R]$.
They are continuously differentiable with continuous, hence integrable,
derivatives. Thus [F7] gives
$$\int_0^R x^ne^{-x}dx=-R^ne^{-R}+n\int_0^R x^{n-1}e^{-x}dx.$$
The endpoint at zero vanishes since $n\ge1$. Taking $R\to\infty$ is
justified by the finite positive improper integrals and the vanishing
boundary term just proved. It gives $M_n=nM_{n-1}$, and induction from
$M_0=1$ gives $M_n=n!$. Finally
$0\le e^{-x}/(1+\lambda x)\le e^{-x}$ for $\lambda\ge0$, so $F(\lambda)$
is finite.

Substituting the formula from step 1.1, the subtracted quantity equals
$$ \frac{\mu^2}{16\pi^2} \log\left(\frac{\mu^2}{\mu_R^2} \frac{\Lambda^2}{\Lambda^2+\mu^2}\right). $$
As $\Lambda\to\infty$, the second factor inside the logarithm tends to $1$;
the limiting logarithm is defined because $\mu^2/\mu_R^2>0$. Continuity of
$\log$ on $(0,\infty)$ proves the stated finite limit.

For every $t\ge0$, finite multiplication of a geometric sum gives
$$ \frac1{1+t}=\sum_{n=0}^N(-t)^n+ (-1)^{N+1}\frac{t^{N+1}}{1+t}. $$
Put $t=\lambda x$, multiply by $e^{-x}$, and integrate. Step 1.2 evaluates
each polynomial moment as $n!$, while the remainder is bounded by
$\lambda^{N+1}M_{N+1}=\lambda^{N+1}(N+1)!$. This gives the exact finite
identity and its stated bound, including $\lambda=0$.

For $\lambda>0$, the magnitudes of successive formal terms have ratio
$\lambda(n+1)$, which eventually exceeds $2$. Thus the terms do not tend to
zero and the power series diverges at every positive $\lambda$; the ratio
test for power-series radius therefore gives radius zero. Separately, the
bare positive coefficient grows quadratically because
$$ \frac{I_\Lambda}{\Lambda^2} =\frac1{16\pi^2}\left( 1-\frac{\mu^2}{\Lambda^2}\log(1+\Lambda^2/\mu^2)\right) \longrightarrow\frac1{16\pi^2}. $$
For the last limit, with $y=1+\Lambda^2/\mu^2$, [F4] gives
$\log y=\int_1^y du/u\le\int_1^y du/\sqrt u\le2\sqrt y$, so the logarithmic
term divided by $\Lambda^2$ tends to zero.

Steps 1.1 and 2.1 give the exact cutoff integral and selected finite
subtraction limit; steps 1.2 and 2.2 prove the finite factorial remainder;
step 2.3 proves that the formal power series diverges for every $\lambda>0$.
These conclusions concern only the two displayed mathematical integrals and
do not assert a full QED renormalization theorem or a continuum limit.

boundaries.evidence: Statement requires a positive cutoff ball. The finite series in step 2.2 has n=0,...,N with N>=0 and hence contains its constant term even at N=0; there is no empty finite truncation.
Step 2.2 includes λ=0 in the finite remainder identity; the denominator remains positive.
Step 1.1 uses μ>0, so the radial denominator never vanishes; the cutoff radius is required positive.
Steps 1.1 and 1.2 evaluate the radial origin and justify the infinite endpoint; step 2.2 includes λ=0.
Step 1.1 carries ACω into the exact radial-measure supplier.

boundaries.reason: Statement of Finite UV subtraction and divergent factorial toy integral: Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and the unit convention of [[def-qft-example-data]]. Let $\mu,\Lambda,\mu_R>0$ have units $\mathrm m^{-1}$. For $k\in\mathbb R^4$, $|k|$ is the Euclidean norm and $\log$ is the natural logarithm. Define the cutoff integral $$ I_\Lambda=\int_{|k|\le\Lambda} \frac{d^4k}{(2\pi)^4(|k|^2+\mu^2)}. $$ Each term in the subtracted expression has units $\mathrm m^{-2}$. Then $$ I_\Lambda= \frac{\Lambda^2-\mu^2\log(1+\Lambda^2/\mu^2)}{16\pi^2}, $$ and the explicitly chosen subtraction has the finite limit $$ \lim_{\Lambda\to\infty} \left(I_\Lambda-\frac{\Lambda^2}{16\pi^2} +\frac{\mu^2}{16\pi^2}\log\frac{\Lambda^2}{\mu_R^2}\right) =\frac{\mu^2}{16\pi^2}\log\frac{\mu^2}{\mu_R^2}. $$ Separately,  The forward iff axis adds no separately stated converse hypothesis here; the recorded claim is the displayed construction, identity, implication or scope qualification, not a characterization by a new necessary-and-sufficient condition.
